The '''Iberian holm oak''' (''Quercus rotundifolia'') is an [[evergreen oak]] native to the western [[Mediterranean region]], with the majority of the population in the [[Iberian Peninsula]] and minor populations in Northwest Africa. The species was [[Species description|first described]] by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] in 1785. It is the typical species of the Iberian ''[[dehesa]]'' or ''montado'', where its sweet-astringent acorns are a source of food for livestock, particularly the [[Iberian pig]]. Its [[acorn]]s have also been used for human nourishment since the [[Neolithic]] era (7,000 BC).<ref name="IOS" /> It is placed in [[Quercus sect. Ilex|section ''Ilex'']].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Denk |first1=Thomas |last2=Grimm |first2=Guido W. |last3=Manos |first3=Paul S. |last4=Deng |first4=Min |last5=Hipp |first5=Andrew L. |date=2017 |title=Appendix 2.1: An updated infrageneric classification of the oaks |website=figshare |doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.5547622.v1 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Appendix_2_1_________An_updated_infrageneric_classification_of_the_oaks/5547622/1 |access-date=2023-02-18 |format=xls |name-list-style=amp }}</ref> Some authors described it as a subspecies of ''[[Quercus ilex]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Quercus rotundifolia'' Lam. (1785) |url=http://www.oaknames.org/search/fullname.asp?id=592 |publisher=International Oak Society |access-date=2023-03-08 |archive-date=2021-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408030117/http://www.oaknames.org/search/fullname.asp?id=592 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:066quercus rotundifolia.JPG|thumb|left|[[Inflorescence]]]]
''Quercus rotundifolia'' is a medium to large tree, usually {{convert|8|-|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} in height, but can reach up to {{convert|15|m|ft|abbr=on}} with a large, dense, rounded [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]]. It has small, leathery, dark-green leaves with a [[glaucous]], densely pubescent underside usually suborbicular to elliptical or lanceolate and are generally spiny to dentate on a younger tree.<ref name="iberica">{{cite web |title=''Quercus rotundifolia'' |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/02_041_03_Quercus.pdf |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=27 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="lauriemeadows">{{cite web |title=Sweet Acorns - ''Quercus rotundifolia'' Lam. |url=http://www.lauriemeadows.info/food_garden/nut/Acorns_Bellota_Quercus_rotundifolia.html |publisher=lauriemeadows.info |access-date=30 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="UE">{{cite web |title=''Quercus rotundifolia'' Lam. Azinheira, azinho, sardão |url=https://www.museubiodiversidade.uevora.pt/elenco-de-especies/biodiversidade-actual/plantas/angiospermicas/quercus-rotundifolia/ |publisher=[[University of Évora]] |access-date=27 December 2020}}</ref> It has a semi-hemispheric [[Calybium and cupule|cupule]].<ref name="UE" />

It flowers from February to April.<ref name="flora-on">{{cite web |title=''Quercus rotundifolia'' Lam. |url=https://flora-on.pt/#/1quercus+rotundifolia |publisher=Flora-on |access-date=30 December 2020}}</ref> Seedlings will start flowering at about eight years old, but they will not start producing acorns until 15 to 20 years old, although trees in humid, good quality soils can start production as early as 10 years.<ref name="lauriemeadows" /> The acorns ripen in autumn, about six months after pollination.<ref name="lauriemeadows" />

It is a resilient tree that can survive temperatures below {{convert|-20|C|F}}, and that on occasion reach {{convert|47|C|F}}.<ref name="IOS">{{cite web |title=Species Spotlight: ''Quercus rotundifolia'' Lam. |date=8 March 2015 |url=https://www.internationaloaksociety.org/content/species-spotlight-quercus-rotundifolia-lam |publisher=International Oak Society |access-date=30 December 2020}}</ref>

As opposed to ''[[Quercus ilex]]'', its acorns have a very low level of bitterness [[tannins]] and so are generally sweet and a good energy source for livestock.<ref name="lauriemeadows" />

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Alentejo 29 5 5 edit.JPG|thumb|left|The tree is often seen on [[dehesa]] biomes typical of [[Alentejo]] (seen here) and [[Extremadura]].]]
''Quercus rotundifolia'' is native to most of the [[Iberian Peninsula]] ([[Portugal]] and [[Spain]]), but is also distributed throughout [[Morocco]], especially in the [[Atlas Mountains]], [[Algeria]], [[Tunisia]], southern [[France]] ([[Languedoc-Roussillon]]) and the [[Balearic Islands]]. It is present in continental, sub-continental or littoral [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean]] areas but always in climatic conditions determined by a fairly hot and dry summer,<ref name="iberica" /> which excludes the wet, oceanic influenced climate of [[Green Spain]] and northwest Portugal, but requires wet winters as the tree is absent from arid climates and those with no real wet months like southeast Spain.<ref name="iberica" /> It grows in a variety of soils and is indifferent to variations in [[edaphic]] conditions, persisting in soils with pH from six to eight.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> The tree is also associated in Iberian holm oak/[[Cedrus atlantica|Atlas cedar]] forests of the [[Atlas Mountains]]. In Morocco, some of these mixed forests are [[habitat]] to the [[endangered]] [[Barbary macaque]].<ref>C. Michael Hogan, 2008</ref>

The tree inhabits dense oak forests, open oak forests and [[dehesa]] ecosystems, from sea level up to {{convert|1900|m|ft|abbr=on}} [[Height above sea level|a.s.l.]]<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> It can live in all altitudes in Portugal, switching with ''[[Quercus suber]]''.<ref name="UE" /> The grasses and herbs beneath it support low-density mixed animal grazing during wetter season(s) and, when the grasses die down in summer, the acorns from the oak trees (at densities of 30 to 50 trees per hectare), plus oak foliage and some retained crops support the animals until the grasses return.<ref name="lauriemeadows" /> It can tolerate frost and short periods of light snow.<ref name="lauriemeadows" />

==Threats==
[[File:Azinheira, Mertola.JPG|thumb|right|Dead Iberian holm oak, [[Mértola]]]]
The species is threatened by the destruction of its habitat for agriculture, [[vineyard]]s and pine or [[eucalyptus]] plantations.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /><ref name="UE" /> Like other perennial oaks in the Iberian Peninsula, ''Quercus rotundifolia'' is also affected by ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'' which is becoming more dangerous due to the increased frequency and duration of droughts associated with [[climate change]] and, especially in Portugal, a decline for the taxa has been reported.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /><ref name="lauriemeadows" /> The tree is also affected by [[wildfires]],<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> though it regenerates well from [[Resprouter|resprouts]].<ref name="lauriemeadows" /> The leaves are eaten by [[Coleophoridae|case moth]] caterpillars, but the tree is not particularly threatened by them.<ref name="lauriemeadows" /> In New Zealand, the caterpillar of the [[puriri moth]] has also been observed to feed on the tree's bark.<ref name="lauriemeadows" /> The tree is notably resistant to [[honey fungus]].<ref name="TPD">{{cite web |title=Temperate Plants Database, Ken Fern |url=http://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Quercus+rotundifolia |publisher=temperate.theferns.info |access-date=30 December 2020}}</ref>

The Iberian holm oak, along with the [[cork oak]], is a protected tree by law in Portugal.<ref>{{cite web |title=Decreto-Lei n.º 169/2001 |work=Diário da República Eletrónico |url=https://dre.pt/pesquisa/-/search/332749/details/maximized |publisher=[[Diário da República]] |access-date=31 December 2020}}</ref>

==Use==
[[File:Dehesa Pigs.jpg|thumb|right|[[Black Iberian pig]]s foraging on ''Q. rotundifolia'']]
The Iberian holm oak's wood is traditionally used to make [[charcoal]]. The acorns can be consumed both by animals and humans. The bark is rich in tannin components for traditional medicinal uses.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /><ref name="lauriemeadows" /> ''Quercus rotundifolia'' is also used as a host plant for the production of both the black truffle (''[[Tuber melanosporum]]'') and the summer truffle ([[Tuber aestivum|''Tuber aestivum'' var ''aestivum'']]).<ref name="lauriemeadows" />

The tree's acorns have been used by humans since the Neolithic era. The inhabitants of the southern Iberian Peninsula 9,000 years ago collected acorns of ''Q. rotundifolia'' in autumn (November), gently toasted them in order to preserve them, ground them in granite mills, and consumed the flour in soups or breads.<ref name="IOS" />

==Notable trees==
[[File:Azinheira da Cova da Iria - Santuário de Fátima - 1.jpg|thumb|left|The Iberian holm oak in the [[Sanctuary of Fátima]] is a tree of public interest in Portugal.]]
An [[Our Lady of Fátima|apparition]] of the [[Blessed Virgin Mary]] over a ''Quercus rotundifolia'' was reported by [[Francisco and Jacinta Marto]] and [[Lúcia dos Santos]] at Fátima in 1916 and 1917. The small tree has since disappeared and its pieces are now [[relic]]s, but other ''Quercus rotundifolia'' near the site persist, one of them being a tree of public interest.<ref>{{cite web |title=Azinheira no santuário de Fátima é uma das 453 árvores classificadas em Portugal |date=9 May 2017 |url=https://www.cmjornal.pt/papa-em-fatima/detalhe/azinheira-no-santuario-de-fatima-e-uma-das-453-arvores-classificadas-em-portugal |publisher=[[Correio da Manhã (Portugal)|Correio da Manhã]] |access-date=27 December 2020}}</ref>
